title: Indexes: when they help, when they hurt and covering indexes

videos.script: This is the lesson people skip to, and it is the one most often half-learned. An index makes a query faster. Everybody knows that sentence, and it hides three things. {{sentence}} The first is what an index is. Not a setting, not a hint — a second copy of some of your columns, kept sorted, with a pointer back to the row. That is why it works, and it is also why it costs. {{copy}} Which is the second thing. Every index you add is paid for on every insert, every update and every delete, for ever. Adding one to make a report faster makes the whole application a little slower, and nobody measures the second half. {{cost}} The third is the one that produces the confusion. You add the index, the query is unchanged, and the database is not using it. There are about six reasons for that and every one of them looks like a bug until you know it. {{unused}} A function around the column. A LIKE starting with a percent sign. A number compared against a text column. And the honest one: the planner looked, and decided reading the whole table was cheaper — which it often is. {{reasons}} We also do the two that give the best return for the least trouble: the composite index, where the order of the columns decides which queries it serves, and the partial index, which covers the rows you actually query. {{best}} And one rule to hang it all on. Do not add an index because it seems likely to help. Add it because you looked, which is the next lesson. {{rule}}
